title: Sequence-Level Knowledge Distillation
hook: Match the teacher's whole output sequence, not just word-by-word probabilities, and the student translation model can drop beam search while running about 10x faster.
key_points: Extends knowledge distillation from the single-token (word) level to the sequence level for neural machine translation.
Trains the student to match the teacher's full output sequences.
Appears to eliminate the need for beam search; the student runs about 10x faster than the teacher with minimal performance loss.
Improves +4.2 BLEU (greedy) and +1.7 BLEU (beam search) over a non-distilled baseline.
With weight pruning, reaches 13x fewer parameters than the teacher with only a 0.4 BLEU decrease.
content_html: Yoon Kim and Alexander M. Rush proposed sequence-level knowledge distillation in June 2016, extending the idea from the single-token (word) level up to whole sequences for neural machine translation. Instead of matching the teacher's per-word probabilities, the student learns to reproduce the teacher's full output sequences.
extra_html:
How it works

Classic distillation matches the teacher's softened distribution one token at a time. Kim and Rush instead train the student against the teacher's complete output sequences, so the student learns the sequences the teacher tends to produce. A useful side effect: the approach appears to eliminate the need for beam search at decode time, letting the student run about 10x faster than the teacher with minimal performance loss.

Why it matters

The authors report gains of +4.2 BLEU with greedy decoding and +1.7 BLEU with beam search over a non-distilled baseline. Combined with weight pruning, the student reaches 13x fewer parameters than the teacher while giving up only 0.4 BLEU - a strong case that distillation can compress sequence models, not just classifiers.

related.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
related.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

related.title: DistilBERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper, Lighter
related.hook: Distill during pre-training instead of after, and you get a general-purpose language model that is 40% smaller and 60% faster while keeping 97% of BERT's understanding.

related.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning
related.hook: Translate a sentence by reading it into one vector, then writing a new sentence out of that vector. This encoder–decoder recipe powered early neural machine translation.
